patches.old: Children progress through the **play stage** (imitating specific roles, like playing "doctor") and the **game stage** (understanding that multiple roles interact according to rules), eventually developing awareness of the **generalized other**
patches.new: Mead described **three** stages, and the exam expects all three in order. In the **preparatory stage** (roughly up to age two) children imitate the actions of those around them without understanding the roles behind them — copying the gesture, not the part. In the **play stage** (roughly two to six) they take **one role at a time**, playing doctor or parent, and so begin to see themselves from another's position. In the **game stage** (roughly seven onward) they can hold **several roles simultaneously** and grasp how those roles interlock, which is what makes organised games possible. It is at this point that the child develops awareness of the **generalized other**

patches.old: Socialization continues in later life, though it increasingly involves **role exit** — the process of disengaging from roles that have been central to one's identity.
patches.new: Socialization continues in later life, though it increasingly involves **role exit** — the process, described by Helen Rose Ebaugh, of disengaging from a role that has been central to one's identity and constructing a new sense of self afterwards. Ebaugh traced four stages: first doubts about the role, seeking alternatives, a turning point at which the exit is made, and creating an "ex-role" identity — the lasting status of being a *former* physician, spouse or member of a faith.

sources.title: OpenStax, Introduction to Sociology 3e §5.1 — theories of self-development, covering Mead's preparatory, play and game stages and the generalized other

visual.title: Agents, stages, and the four types
visual.alt: A timeline from birth to later life with bars showing when family, peers, school, media and work act as socialization agents and what each transmits; three cards for Mead's preparatory, play and game stages with their ages and defining feature; and four cards distinguishing anticipatory socialization, developmental socialization, resocialization and role exit by what is happening to the role the person holds.
visual.caption: Mead's stages go imitation, then one role at a time, then several roles at once — the last is what makes a game, and the generalized other, possible.
